title.en: King Arthur and Ramayana: ancient stories that speak to the moral dilemmas of today’s leaders

hook.en: Across ancient India and medieval Britain, two legendary rulers face the same choice: sacrifice their love or shatter the moral foundation of their kingdom.

sections.body_en: The ancient Hindu epic *Ramayana* (attributed to Valmiki, 750-500BC) tells the story of Rama, prince and eventual king of Ayodhya, and his struggle to rescue his wife Sita after her abduction by the demon-king Ravana. T.H. White’s *The Once and Future King* (1958) retells the Arthurian legend, the round table, and the love triangle between Arthur, his queen, Guenever, and the knight Lancelot. Separated by centuries, both epics ask whether the king should let his queen burn. This separates the morality of the husband from the duty of the leader. After rescuing Sita and slaying Ravana, Rama initially rejects his wife. As king, he must reckon with public morality. Sita demands a test by fire, pleading with the god of fire not to let her burn if she is faithful, and walks into the flames unscathed. Guenever is unfaithful to Arthur. Arthur has made peace with her relationship with Lancelot, but when other knights catch them in adultery, Arthur orders Guenever burnt at the stake to uphold public morality. Both are bringers of a moral code. Arthur replaces brute force with a system of justice through his Round Table. Rama establishes Ram-Rajya, a state of righteousness and equality before the law. Faced with the choice between breaking moral codes or letting their queens burn, they uphold the morality of their kingdoms at great personal cost. Lancelot rescues Guenever, and fire refuses to burn Sita, but both kings endure suffering. White’s Arthur laments that if Lancelot rescues her, innocent guards will die, and if they do not, his beloved Gwen will burn. Valmiki’s Rama justifies himself before the three worlds, stating that without purification, virtuous people would call him foolish and driven by desire. Arthur’s system would have burnt Guenever alive without Lancelot, and Rama’s Ram-Rajya leads to the unfair treatment of Sita. Good triumphs when the prevailing moral order is defied.

When Joe Biden granted an “unconditional” presidential pardon to his son Hunter Biden for tax and gun-related offences in 2024, critics accused him of abusing public power to protect his own family.

Weeks later, on his first day back in office, Donald Trump granted sweeping clemency to nearly 1,600 people charged with or convicted of offences stemming from the January 6 Capitol attack.

The circumstances might be different, but the dilemma is very much the same that we find in Valmiki and T.H White’s texts: do our leaders have the right to a private morality?

It is their capacity to ask such profound and enduring questions that has kept both the Ramayana and the legend of King Arthur alive across centuries. Both stories have and will be retold by each generation and will continue to return as novels, films, TV series and graphic novels.

For anyone wishing to enter these wonderful worlds, my recommendation would be to begin with T. H. White’s The Once and Future King and Valmiki’s Ramayana, available in an excellent English translation by Bibek Debroy. Read together, they show why the epics still matter. They don’t give us easy answers, but they teach us how to ask better questions.

As part of the Rethinking the Classics series, we’re asking our experts to recommend a book or artwork that tackles similar themes to the canonical work in question, but isn’t (yet) considered a classic itself. Here is Harsh Trivedi’s suggestion:

May Our Joy Endure by Laura-Ève Lambert (2022) explores the moral contradictions of power through the character of Céline Wachowski.

Wachowski is a celebrated architect based in Montreal who gets “cancelled” following an exposé on the malpractices of her architectural firm. The novel explores a complex dilemma: can someone be both responsible for injustice and a victim of it?

Like Rama and Arthur, Wachowski finds herself caught between her personal convictions and the judgment of others. But unlike the two kings, who sacrifice their personal happiness in the name of public morality, Wachowski attempts to use her privilege to define what is right and influence the public narrative in her favour.

summary.vi: Bài viết khám phá những tình thế tiến thoái lưỡng nan về đạo đức của các nhà lãnh đạo qua hai tác phẩm kinh điển là sử thi Ramayana của Ấn Độ và truyền thuyết vua Arthur từ nước Anh trung cổ. Cả hai vị vua Rama và Arthur đều phải đối mặt với lựa chọn đau đớn giữa tình cảm cá nhân dành cho người bạn đời và nghĩa vụ duy trì trật tự công lý của vương quốc. Dù cách biệt về thời gian và văn hóa, những câu chuyện này vẫn phản ánh chính xác các cuộc tranh luận hiện đại về quyền lực, trách nhiệm và giới hạn của đạo đức cá nhân trước công chúng.

keyPoint.en: Like a captain steering a ship through a violent storm, leaders navigate impossible choices between personal loyalty and public duty. [p:Reflect on a recent decision where you balanced personal relationships with strict fairness.] What core values guide your actions when the rules demand a heavy personal sacrifice?
keyPoint.vi: Giống như người thuyền trưởng lái con tàu qua cơn bão dữ, các nhà lãnh đạo phải điều hướng giữa lòng trung thành cá nhân và trách nhiệm công cộng. [p:Hãy suy ngẫm về một quyết định gần đây khi bạn cân bằng các mối quan hệ cá nhân với sự công bằng.] Những giá trị cốt lõi nào dẫn dắt hành động của bạn khi quy tắc đòi hỏi sự hy sinh cá nhân?

en: Identify a recent situation where personal loyalty conflicted with an established rule.
List the potential consequences of prioritizing personal relationships over shared standards.
Write down one guiding principle to maintain fairness in future difficult choices.
vi: Xác định một tình huống gần đây khi lòng trung thành cá nhân mâu thuẫn với một quy tắc đã thiết lập.
Liệt kê các hậu quả tiềm ẩn của việc ưu tiên mối quan hệ cá nhân hơn tiêu chuẩn chung.
Viết ra một nguyên tắc chỉ đạo để duy trì sự công bằng trong các lựa chọn khó khăn sắp tới.
